reconcile.connective: JFB reads Luke's 'in a moment of time' as marking a supernaturally extended vision, not a literal naked-eye panorama requiring any particular earth-shape.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptics' Annotated Bible takes the mountain-top vista at face value, quipping of Matthew 4:8: "I guess the earth was flat in those days."

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, comment on Matthew 4:8 (skepticsannotatedbible.com/mt/4.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; mt/4.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: But to limit this to the most extensive scene which the natural eye could take in, is to give a sense to the expression, "all the kingdoms of the world," quite violent. It remains, then, to gather from the expression, "in a moment of time"-- which manifestly is intended to intimate some supernatural operation—that it was permitted to the tempter to extend preternaturally for a moment our Lord's range of vision, and throw a "glory" or glitter over the scene of vision …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB denies the mountain scene was a literal naked-eye panorama, defusing the claim that Matthew's narrative presupposes flat-earth geometry.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on Matthew 4:8
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this exact verse, reading the 'moment of time' clause as marking a supernaturally extended vision rather than ordinary sight — the standard harmonization of the geometry objection.
